title: Buttons are back and storage is king when it comes to car interiors
gist: Nissan design manager Hiren Patel says the industry's move to switchless, Piano Black interiors drew complaints about distraction, and the new Rogue Hybrid brings back buttons and storage. The article frames pushback against touchscreen-everything design as working.

insights.claim: Automakers removed physical switches and moved controls to software believing it would save money and tooling for unique parts and make interiors more like a software experience.
insights.speaker: Hiren Patel
insights.so_what: Cost-driven software-defined cabin design is being reconsidered as customer complaints mount.
insights.quote: We can put it all in the software. It’ll save money.

insights.claim: Customers complained that touch-only controls take eyes off the road to change temperature or adjust seats, and are less intuitive than a phone.
insights.speaker: Hiren Patel
insights.so_what: User-experience backlash is steering design back to physical controls.

insights.claim: Rising complexity of subsystems means menus differ by automaker, and Patel says nobody has figured out a great way of doing it.
insights.speaker: Hiren Patel
insights.so_what: No dominant UI standard exists, leaving room for differentiation.

insights.claim: The author concludes that pushback against minimalist, touch-heavy interiors seems to be working.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Trend implies buttons-and-storage as a selling point in coming model cycles.
insights.locator: As with interior design for houses

themes.theme: Nissan Rogue Hybrid as a case study

insights.claim: The new Rogue Hybrid, redesigned under Patel for Nissan's bestselling family SUV, is less minimalist than the all-electric Ariya, with buttons and switches for most controls, built-in storage, puffer-jacket-inspired seats and no Piano Black.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A top-volume nameplate adopting physical controls is a signal for mainstream segments.

insights.claim: Patel says customers want easy intuitive controls, wireless charging, easy-to-clean surfaces, lots of storage and easy access, so rear doors open to 90 degrees for child seats and elderly passengers.
insights.speaker: Hiren Patel
insights.so_what: Family-segment priorities differ from image-conscious sedan buyers, shaping segment-specific design.

insights.claim: Patel says designing an everyday product that is beautiful is challenging because of cost, engineering, usability and feasibility constraints, requiring fights over every millimeter.
insights.speaker: Hiren Patel
insights.so_what: Illustrates tight cost trade-offs behind interior design choices.
